title: Association between duodenal mucosa-associated periodontal bacteria and advanced liver fibrosis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
content:
by Kazuki Niida, Yasunori Yamamoto, Teruki Miyake, Mirai Hayashi, Kazuhiro Tange, Takao Watanabe, Osamu Yoshida, Yoshio Tokumoto, Hideomi Tomida, Eiji Takeshita, Yoshio Ikeda, Yoichi Hiasa

Gut microbiota and periodontal diseases are potential risk factors for duodenal mucosa-associated microbiota in fibrosis progression of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease; however, the specific contribution of duodenal mucosa-associated microbiota remains unclear. Therefore, in this prospective study, we investigated its association with liver stiffness to elucidate its role in disease progression. Duodenal brush samples were collected during endoscopy from patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, classified by liver stiffness measurement into advanced (liver stiffness measurement>8.7 kPa, n = 10) and non-advanced (n = 20) groups. Extracted DNA was subjected to shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Analyses included taxonomy, diversity, differential abundance (edgeR), correlation (Spearman), and receiver operating characteristic predictive modeling, focusing on periodontal bacteria. While microbial diversity did not differ, advanced metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease was characterized by the enrichment of the phylum Pseudomonadota and the genera Haemophilus and Klebsiella. Eight periodontal bacteria, including Campylobacter rectus, Porphyromonas gingivalis, and Fusobacterium nucleatum, were significantly enriched in patients with advanced metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (P < 0.05) and correlated with liver fibrosis markers. A model based on these bacteria discriminated advanced metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease with an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI, 0.634–1.000). Duodenal mucosa-associated microbiota alterations, particularly the enrichment of eight periodontal species, were associated with fibrosis severity. These findings highlight the role of the oral-gut-liver axis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease progression and suggest potential microbial biomarkers and therapeutic targets.
